title: “YOUR LIPS DRIP NECTAR”: Why Does Scripture Describe Romantic Attraction This Sensually?
paragraphs: “YOUR LIPS DRIP NECTAR”: Why Does Scripture Describe Romantic Attraction This Sensually?
Song of Songs 4:11 is the kind of Bible verse people rarely read from the pulpit—and perhaps that says more about us than it does about God.
Not tucked away in some forbidden ancient love poem.
Not smuggled into Scripture by mistake.
Not a sentence God somehow forgot to edit out.
Right in the Song of Songs.
And the Hebrew is arguably even more vivid than some English translations allow you to feel:

נֹפֶת תִּטֹּפְנָה שִׂפְתוֹתַיִךְ כַּלָּה
דְּבַשׁ וְחָלָב תַּחַת לְשׁוֹנֵךְ
Nōp̄eṯ tiṭṭōp̄ənāh śip̄ṯōṯayiḵ, kallāh; dəḇaš wəḥālāḇ taḥaṯ ləšōnēḵ.
“Your lips, my bride, drip nectar; honey and milk are under your tongue…”
Because if you grew up believing that holiness required Christians to become embarrassed whenever romantic attraction entered the conversation, this verse can feel almost scandalous.
And God allowed all of it into Holy Scripture.
That question takes us somewhere much deeper than romance.
It takes us into the wreckage of what sin has done to human desire—and into the astonishing beauty of what God intended desire to be before we corrupted it.
Because perhaps the scandal is not that Scripture can speak this sensually.
Perhaps the scandal is that sin has distorted sexuality so thoroughly that we struggle to imagine sensuality without impurity.
And if we miss it, we may spend our lives calling something dirty that God created beautiful while simultaneously tolerating versions of desire that God calls destructive.
The word נֹפֶת — nōp̄eṯ refers to flowing or dripping honey, sweetness associated with the honeycomb.
Then comes תִּטֹּפְנָה — tiṭṭōp̄ənāh, from the Hebrew root נטף — nāṭap̄, carrying the idea of dripping, dropping, or distilling.
The poet could have said, “You are attractive.”
And the surrounding passage becomes even more sensory.
The beloved is compared with a garden, fruit, spices, perfume, flowing water, pomegranates, nard, saffron, cinnamon, myrrh, aloes, and Lebanon.
You can almost smell the poetry.
Biblical Hebrew poetry does not merely inform the intellect here.
Because God created human beings with senses.
God created the eye that notices beauty.
God created the nose that recognizes fragrance.
The capacity to look at another human being within the covenantal goodness God designed and say, in effect…
There is nothing inherently unholy about those words.
The tragedy is what humanity has done with them.
Go all the way back to Genesis.
Before people learned to swipe past one another as though human beings were disposable merchandise.
Genesis 2:25 tells us that the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
And almost immediately, nakedness became entangled with hiding.
That should break something inside us.
Because one of sin's earliest achievements was taking what had existed without shame and surrounding it with fear.
Human beings have been hiding ever since.
Sometimes behind marriages where two people sleep inches apart but have not felt emotionally known in years.
And maybe that is why Song of Songs can make religious people uncomfortable.
It refuses to pretend that embodied human love does not exist.
But it also refuses to treat desire the way our culture often treats it.
The Song does not reduce the beloved to a body for consumption.
Again and again, attraction exists alongside admiration, exclusivity, tenderness, delight, longing, belonging, and covenant-shaped language.
Notice the word immediately following the description of her lips:
The sensuality is not floating in moral emptiness.
A few verses earlier the man says, “You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride” (Song of Songs 4:9).
Then, immediately after the nectar, honey, milk, and fragrance imagery, comes another striking picture:
גַּן נָעוּל אֲחֹתִי כַלָּה… מַעְיָן חָתוּם
Gan nāʿūl, ʾaḥōṯî kallāh… maʿyān ḥāṯūm.
Whatever interpretive questions surround every detail of this extraordinary poem, one thing should be impossible to miss:
Biblical desire is not presented as indiscriminate consumption.
And that is almost the opposite of what lust teaches.
I want your body without carrying the weight of your soul.
That distinction may expose something uncomfortable.
Because you can technically avoid adultery while allowing lust to colonize your imagination.
You can attend church on Sunday and spend Monday feeding desires you would be terrified for anyone to discover.
You can know worship songs by heart and still secretly use people in your imagination.
You can preach purity publicly while privately starving for images that slowly teach your brain to treat human beings as products.
And perhaps the most frightening part is how normal it can begin to feel.
One conversation you know has crossed a boundary.
Until eventually the person in the mirror knows exactly where to hide.
But Jesus does not merely address what our bodies do.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Christ takes the command against adultery and drives it beneath external behavior into lustful intention.
Because suddenly the question is no longer simply:
“What have I been teaching my heart to desire?”
And now Song of Songs becomes even more remarkable.
Because Christianity's answer to corrupted desire is not that beauty must become ugly.
God does not need to apologize for creating attraction.
We need forgiveness for corrupting it.
There are people reading this who know exactly what that means.
Maybe your sexuality carries memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe pornography has followed you for years.
Maybe you became the person you once promised yourself you would never become.
You smile when people see you at church.
But there is another version of your life behind the locked door.
And when everything becomes quiet, shame starts preaching.
And this is where the Gospel becomes infinitely greater than religious embarrassment.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to teach sexually broken people better behavior.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for an edited version of you.
The thing you have never said aloud.
He knew the entire record before the nails entered His hands.
And He went to the cross anyway.
That does not make sin small.
It reveals how enormous grace is.
The cross is not God saying your sin never mattered.
The cross is God demonstrating exactly how seriously sin mattered—and how far His redeeming love was willing to go.
So repentance is not crawling toward a Savior who would rather you stayed away.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One whose mercy sinners could never purchase.
You do not repent because Christ hates you.
You repent because sin is killing what Christ came to restore.
That means the person trapped in pornography does not have to make peace with chains.
The adulterer does not have to make adultery an identity.
The sexually wounded do not have to believe what happened to them determines their worth.
The ashamed do not have to spend the rest of their lives hiding from God.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
Not cheap grace that whispers, “Keep doing whatever you want.”
Grace that finds you in the mud and loves you too much to leave you there.
Maybe that is what makes Song of Songs 4:11 so unexpectedly beautiful.
Those words do not belong to pornography.
God created beauty before Satan ever learned to counterfeit it.
God created intimacy before humanity learned to exploit it.
God created desire before sin taught us to worship it.
God created marriage before culture learned to trivialize it.
And Scripture is not embarrassed about the goodness of what God made.
But neither should we confuse God's design with every desire our fallen hearts happen to produce.
Christian holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is the surrender of the whole person—body included—to God.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Christ.
Even the parts you are ashamed to name.
Because Jesus does not redeem us by pretending our scandals never happened.
He redeems us by entering the story and writing an ending sin could never produce.
Then stop performing for one moment.
Did a sentence land somewhere you hoped nobody would touch?
Then perhaps your response does not need to be sophisticated.
Maybe it needs to be surrender.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
Christ purchased redemption, not your comment.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop protecting the darkness.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not the only believer fighting a battle behind a smile.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Someone's marriage may be hanging by a thread.
Someone may have pornography open in another tab.
Someone may believe sexual failure has placed them permanently outside the reach of Christ.
Someone may need to discover tonight that conviction is not the same thing as condemnation—and that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Some truths need to be read again when temptation gets loud.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow as well.
But hear this carefully, because truth matters more than fundraising:
Scripture gives us a better foundation than pressure.
Paul writes that giving should be “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης — mē ex anankēs
Not because somebody manipulated your guilt.
Not because somebody frightened you into believing God's favor has a monthly price.
The Gospel is not behind a paywall.
But believers can freely choose to support Gospel work they believe is bearing good fruit.
And whether or not you can financially support the ministry, you can still help.
Send it privately to someone fighting temptation.
Send it to the single Christian trying to understand desire without being ruled by it.
Send it to the believer drowning in pornography who thinks God is finished with them.
Send it to the wounded person who has confused what someone did to them with who they are.
Because the final message of Christianity is not that good people successfully avoided scandal.
The message is that sinners can be redeemed by a crucified and risen Savior.
The Bible can describe a bride's lips dripping nectar without embarrassment because God is not embarrassed by the goodness of His creation.
He is opposed to what sin does to it.
And Jesus Christ came not merely to cover our shame with religious language, but to reconcile sinners to God and begin making broken people new.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot seem to control.
Bring Him the part of your story you are convinced would make everybody leave.
And discover that the Savior who knows the ugliest chapter is still capable of writing holiness into the pages that remain.
Because perhaps the most scandalous thing in this entire story was never that Scripture said, “Your lips drip nectar.”
Perhaps the greater scandal is that Jesus looked at sinners covered in shame…
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but once Jesus takes the pen, it does not get to write the ending.
